title: The other day
description: A few days ago, without saying exactly when.
details:
Example: I saw Sam at the station the other day.

Usage: Use for a recent event in the past, not for tomorrow.

title: Guess what?
description: I have some news that may surprise you.
details:
Example: Guess what? I got the job!

Usage: An informal way to get someone’s attention before sharing news.

title: I was just about to…
description: I was going to do something very soon.
details:
Example: I was just about to leave when you called.

Usage: Often followed by when and an event that interrupted the plan.

title: At first
description: At the beginning, before something changed.
details:
Example: At first, I thought it was a joke.

Usage: Usually followed later by what changed.

title: I was on my way to…
description: I was travelling towards a place.
details:
Example: I was on my way to work when you called.

Usage: Follow with a place. Leave out to before home: on my way home.

title: After that
description: Following the event I just mentioned.
details:
Example: We checked in. After that, we went out for dinner.

Usage: Use to move to the next part of a story.

title: While I was…
description: During an activity I was doing.
details:
Example: While I was cooking, the phone rang.

Usage: Follow with an -ing form to describe an activity in progress.

title: All of a sudden
description: Something happened very suddenly.
details:
Example: All of a sudden, the lights went out.

Usage: Useful for an unexpected change in a story.

title: I didn’t expect that
description: Something surprised me.
details:
Example: She offered to pay. I didn’t expect that.

Usage: Use after explaining what happened.

title: It turns out…
description: I’ve discovered something I didn’t know before.
details:
Example: It turns out we live on the same street.

Usage: Use turned out when telling a story entirely in the past.

title: I ended up…
description: This was what I finally did, often without planning it.
details:
Example: I ended up walking home.

Usage: Follow with an -ing form or a place: ended up at the wrong station.

title: By the time…
description: When this moment arrived, something else had happened.
details:
Example: By the time we got there, the shop had closed.

Usage: Use to connect the timing of two events.

title: I nearly…
description: I almost did something, but didn’t.
details:
Example: I nearly missed the train.

Usage: The example means you caught the train, but only just.

title: Luckily…
description: Something happened that helped or prevented a problem.
details:
Example: Luckily, I had a spare key.

Usage: Introduce the fortunate part of the situation.

title: The problem was…
description: This was the difficulty we faced.
details:
Example: The problem was, I didn’t have his number.

Usage: Use to explain what made the situation difficult.

title: Nothing went to plan
description: Everything happened differently from what I intended.
details:
Example: We left late and got lost. Nothing went to plan.

Usage: Useful for summarising a series of problems or unexpected changes.

title: In the end
description: This was the final result after everything that happened.
details:
Example: In the end, we stayed home.

Usage: Use for the outcome of a situation or decision.

title: At the time
description: Back then, rather than with what I know now.
details:
Example: At the time, I thought it was a good idea.

Usage: Useful when your view has changed since the event.

title: Looking back
description: Thinking about a past situation now.
details:
Example: Looking back, I should have asked for help.

Usage: Introduce what you now think about an earlier experience.

title: Long story short
description: I’ll skip the details and give you the result.
details:
Example: Long story short, we missed the train.

Usage: Informal; useful when a story has become lengthy.
